contaminants.name: Microplastics
contaminants.description: Tiny plastic particles less than 5 millimeters in size. Found in drinking water worldwide. Currently unregulated in the United States despite growing health concerns.
contaminants.healthEffects: Emerging research links microplastic ingestion to inflammation, endocrine disruption, and cellular damage. Particle size determines whether they cross the gut and lung barriers.
contaminants.sources: Plastic packaging, synthetic textiles, tire wear, breakdown of larger plastic debris, water treatment processes that cannot filter sub-micron particles.
contaminants.rarityNote: Almost no public drinking-water databases track microplastics — the EWG Tap Water Database, EPA SDWIS, and most state portals omit it entirely because there is no federal limit and no routine monitoring requirement. A Ripples Effect tracks it anyway.

contaminants.name: Arsenic
contaminants.description: A naturally occurring element widely distributed in the Earth's crust. An EPA-classified human carcinogen.
contaminants.healthEffects: Long-term exposure causes skin, bladder, and lung cancer. Also linked to cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and reduced cognitive function in children.
contaminants.sources: Natural deposits in bedrock, industrial runoff, agricultural pesticides, smelting.

contaminants.name: E. coli / Coliform
contaminants.description: Fecal indicator bacteria that signal sewage or animal waste contamination. Any detectable level in treated drinking water is a violation.
contaminants.healthEffects: Causes severe gastrointestinal illness, diarrhea, and in some strains (O157:H7) kidney failure and death. Especially dangerous for young children and the elderly.
contaminants.sources: Sewage overflows, agricultural runoff (manure), failing septic systems, wildlife contamination.
contaminants.rarityNote: Critical for untreated surface water monitoring — rarely tracked in consumer databases.

contaminants.name: Lead
contaminants.description: A neurotoxic heavy metal that enters drinking water primarily through corrosion of plumbing materials.
contaminants.healthEffects: Especially harmful to children — causes irreversible neurological damage, lowered IQ, behavioral problems, and anemia. No safe level of exposure exists.
contaminants.sources: Lead service lines, brass fixtures, lead solder in plumbing, galvanized pipes.
contaminants.rarityNote: Tracked by EWG and EPA, but service-line inventory data is still incomplete nationwide.

contaminants.name: PFOA (Perfluorooctanoic acid)
contaminants.description: A "forever chemical" in the PFAS family. Does not break down in the environment or human body.
contaminants.healthEffects: Linked to kidney and testicular cancer, thyroid disease, immune suppression, pregnancy-induced hypertension, and low birth weight.
contaminants.sources: Industrial discharges, firefighting foam (AFFF), stain-resistant carpets, non-stick cookware manufacturing, waterproof textiles.
contaminants.rarityNote: Only regulated as of 2024 (EPA MCL of 4 ppt). EWG tracks; many state portals still do not.

contaminants.name: PFOS (Perfluorooctane sulfonate)
contaminants.description: A persistent PFAS compound used in fire-fighting foams and stain repellents.
contaminants.healthEffects: Associated with liver damage, immune effects, thyroid disruption, and decreased fertility.
contaminants.sources: Aqueous film-forming foams (AFFF), textile treatments, paper coatings, chrome plating.
contaminants.rarityNote: Newly regulated in 2024. Limited historical data exists.

contaminants.name: Atrazine
contaminants.description: One of the most widely used agricultural herbicides in the United States, banned in the EU.
contaminants.healthEffects: Endocrine disruptor that alters hormone levels; linked to reproductive harm and birth defects.
contaminants.sources: Corn and sugarcane herbicide runoff.

contaminants.name: Chlorine (Free)
contaminants.description: Most common drinking water disinfectant in the United States.
contaminants.healthEffects: Can react with organic matter to form disinfection byproducts; some people are sensitive to chlorine taste and odor.
contaminants.sources: Added at water treatment plants for pathogen control.

contaminants.name: Chromium-6 (Hexavalent Chromium)
contaminants.description: The cancer-causing chemical made famous by the film "Erin Brockovich." Regulated only as total chromium.
contaminants.healthEffects: Known human carcinogen when inhaled; linked to stomach and intestinal cancer when ingested.
contaminants.sources: Industrial discharge from steel and pulp mills, electroplating, leather tanning, natural erosion.

contaminants.name: Copper
contaminants.description: A metal that enters drinking water through corrosion of copper plumbing. Also naturally occurring in some water sources.
contaminants.healthEffects: Short-term exposure causes gastrointestinal distress. Long-term exposure damages liver and kidneys. Wilson's disease patients are especially at risk.
contaminants.sources: Copper pipes and plumbing corrosion, industrial discharges, mining runoff, natural deposits.

contaminants.name: Glyphosate
contaminants.description: The most widely used herbicide in the world, best known by the brand name Roundup. The EPA legal limit is 700 ppb, far above health guidelines.
contaminants.healthEffects: Classified as a probable human carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC). Linked to non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
contaminants.sources: Agricultural herbicide runoff, urban and suburban lawn care, forestry applications.
contaminants.rarityNote: EPA MCL (700 ppb) is 140x higher than the health guideline.

contaminants.name: Haloacetic Acids (HAA5)
contaminants.description: A group of five haloacetic acid compounds formed as disinfection byproducts.
contaminants.healthEffects: Linked to cancer and potential developmental harm during pregnancy.
contaminants.sources: Chlorination and chloramination disinfection processes.

contaminants.name: Mercury
contaminants.description: A toxic heavy metal that bioaccumulates in fish and persists in the environment. Methylmercury is the most dangerous form.
contaminants.healthEffects: Neurotoxic. Damages the brain, kidneys, and developing fetus. Children are especially vulnerable to cognitive and motor impairment.
contaminants.sources: Coal-fired power plant emissions, mining runoff, industrial waste, natural deposits, abandoned gold mines.

contaminants.name: Nitrate
contaminants.description: A nitrogen compound that enters water from fertilizer runoff and septic systems.
contaminants.healthEffects: Infants under 6 months can develop methemoglobinemia ("blue baby syndrome"), which can be fatal.
contaminants.sources: Synthetic fertilizer, manure, septic systems, sewage, atmospheric deposition.

contaminants.name: Radium (combined 226/228)
contaminants.description: A naturally occurring radioactive element that dissolves from rock into groundwater. Found in many Midwest and Northeast aquifers.
contaminants.healthEffects: Long-term exposure increases risk of bone cancer, lymphoma, and leukemia. Children are especially vulnerable.
contaminants.sources: Natural erosion of uranium-bearing rocks and minerals in aquifers.

contaminants.name: Total Trihalomethanes (TTHM)
contaminants.description: Formed when chlorine disinfectant reacts with natural organic matter in source water.
contaminants.healthEffects: Increased cancer risk (especially bladder cancer), potential reproductive and developmental issues.
contaminants.sources: Chlorination of water containing organic matter; levels rise during warm seasons.

contaminants.name: Trichloroethylene (TCE)
contaminants.description: A volatile organic compound used as an industrial solvent and degreaser. Made famous by the Woburn, MA contamination case (book/film "A Civil Action").
contaminants.healthEffects: Known human carcinogen (kidney, liver, cervical cancer). Also linked to heart defects in fetuses and Parkinson's disease.
contaminants.sources: Metal degreasing, dry cleaning, adhesive and paint manufacturing, industrial spills and improper disposal.

contaminants.name: Uranium
contaminants.description: A naturally occurring radioactive element found in some groundwater.
contaminants.healthEffects: Kidney toxicity and elevated cancer risk from long-term alpha radiation exposure.
contaminants.sources: Natural uranium-bearing rocks and minerals; mining and milling wastes.

contaminants.name: 1,4-Dioxane
contaminants.description: A likely human carcinogen found in industrial solvents and as a contaminant in many consumer products. Detected in water systems serving over 100 million Americans.
contaminants.healthEffects: Classified as a probable human carcinogen. Long-term exposure may cause liver and kidney damage.
contaminants.sources: Industrial solvent manufacturing, chemical plant discharges, landfill leachate, consumer product contamination.
contaminants.rarityNote: Detected in water systems serving over 100 million Americans. No federal MCL.

contaminants.name: Manganese
contaminants.description: A naturally occurring metal found in rocks and soil. While essential in trace amounts, elevated levels in water are a concern. Unregulated in drinking water.
contaminants.healthEffects: Long-term exposure causes neurological effects, including tremors, muscle stiffness, and cognitive impairment (manganism).
contaminants.sources: Natural erosion of rocks and soil, mining runoff, industrial discharges, well water.
contaminants.rarityNote: No federal MCL. EPA has a lifetime health advisory of 300 ppb.

contaminants.name: Perchlorate
contaminants.description: A rocket fuel component that has contaminated drinking water in at least 45 states. Unregulated at the federal level despite EPA determination that it meets the criteria for regulation.
contaminants.healthEffects: Disrupts thyroid hormone production by blocking iodine uptake. Especially harmful to pregnant women, fetuses, and infants.
contaminants.sources: Rocket fuel manufacturing, military bases, fireworks, flares, aerospace industry.
contaminants.rarityNote: EPA issued a regulatory determination in 2011 but has not yet set an MCL.

contaminants.name: PFBS (Perfluorobutane sulfonate)
contaminants.description: A shorter-chain PFAS compound used as a replacement for PFOS. Persists in the environment and human body, though shorter than PFOA/PFOS.
contaminants.healthEffects: Linked to thyroid effects, delayed development in offspring, and kidney effects. Shorter-chain PFAS are harder to filter.
contaminants.sources: Stain-resistant treatments, firefighting foams, food packaging, industrial processes.
contaminants.rarityNote: Shorter-chain PFAS replacement. Not yet individually regulated.

utilities.name: City of Phoenix Water Services Department
utilities.notes: Sources: Salt River Project, Colorado River (via CAP), and groundwater.

utilities.name: Los Angeles Department of Water and Power
utilities.notes: Sources: LA Aqueduct (Owens Valley), California Aqueduct, Colorado River Aqueduct, local groundwater.

utilities.name: San Diego Water Department
utilities.notes: Sources: Imported (Colorado River, Northern CA) and local surface water.

utilities.name: San Francisco Public Utilities Commission
utilities.notes: Source: Hetch Hetchy Reservoir (Yosemite) with local reservoirs. Mostly unfiltered, UV + chlorine.

utilities.name: Denver Water
utilities.notes: Sources: South Platte River, Blue River, Williams Fork River, Fraser River, Ralston Creek.

utilities.name: Miami-Dade Water and Sewer Department
utilities.notes: Sources: Biscayne Aquifer (groundwater).

utilities.name: City of Atlanta Department of Watershed Management
utilities.notes: Sources: Chattahoochee River and Lake Lanier.

utilities.name: City of Chicago Department of Water Management
utilities.notes: Draws from Lake Michigan, one of the largest surface water systems in the US.

utilities.name: Citizens Energy Group (Indianapolis Water)
utilities.notes: Sources: White River, Fall Creek, Geist Reservoir, Morse Reservoir, and groundwater aquifers.

utilities.name: New Orleans Sewerage and Water Board
utilities.notes: Source: Mississippi River. Vulnerable to storm surges and infrastructure failures.

utilities.name: Massachusetts Water Resources Authority
utilities.notes: Source: Quabbin and Wachusett Reservoirs. Serves 3.1 million people in Greater Boston.

utilities.name: City of Flint Water Department
utilities.notes: Flint River source. Site of the 2014-2019 lead contamination crisis after source water switch without corrosion control.

utilities.name: Detroit Water and Sewerage Department
utilities.notes: Source: Detroit River. Serves most of Southeast Michigan. Also supplied Flint before the 2014 switch.

utilities.name: City of Minneapolis Water Treatment & Distribution
utilities.notes: Source: Mississippi River. Ultrafiltration + granular activated carbon treatment.

utilities.name: City of St. Louis Water Division
utilities.notes: Sources: Missouri and Mississippi Rivers. Two treatment plants serving the city.

utilities.name: Charlotte Water
utilities.notes: Source: Catawba River (Mountain Island Lake and Lake Norman).

utilities.name: Newark Department of Water and Sewer Utilities
utilities.notes: Source: Pequannock/Wanaque watersheds. Experienced elevated lead levels in 2016-2019 due to lead service lines.

utilities.name: Las Vegas Valley Water District
utilities.notes: Source: Lake Mead (Colorado River). Facing declining water levels due to prolonged drought.

utilities.name: New York City Department of Environmental Protection
utilities.notes: Sources: Catskill/Delaware and Croton watersheds. Mostly unfiltered, UV + chlorine disinfection.

utilities.name: City of Columbus Division of Water
utilities.notes: Sources: Scioto River and Big Walnut Creek.

utilities.name: Greater Cincinnati Water Works
utilities.notes: Sources: Ohio River and Great Miami Aquifer. Pioneered granular activated carbon treatment.

utilities.name: Portland Water Bureau
utilities.notes: Source: Bull Run Watershed. Unfiltered, UV + chlorine disinfection. Among cleanest large systems in US.

utilities.name: Pittsburgh Water and Sewer Authority
utilities.notes: Source: Allegheny River. Experienced lead exceedances and violations 2016-2019.

utilities.name: Philadelphia Water Department
utilities.notes: Sources: Schuylkill and Delaware Rivers.

utilities.name: Metro Nashville Water Services
utilities.notes: Source: Cumberland River (J. Percy Priest Lake and Old Hickory Lake).

utilities.name: Fort Worth Water Department
utilities.notes: Draws from Lake Worth, Eagle Mountain Lake, Lake Bridgeport, and Cedar Creek Reservoir.

utilities.name: Dallas Water Utilities
utilities.notes: Sources: Ray Hubbard, Lewisville, Grapevine, Ray Roberts, and Tawakoni lakes.

utilities.name: City of Houston Public Works
utilities.notes: Sources: Lake Houston, Lake Conroe, Trinity River.

utilities.name: Seattle Public Utilities
utilities.notes: Sources: Cedar River and Tolt River watersheds.

utilities.name: Milwaukee Water Works
utilities.notes: Source: Lake Michigan. Site of 1993 Cryptosporidium outbreak, largest waterborne disease outbreak in US history.
